#define HOST_DEVICE        
#define HOST_DEVICE_INLINE inline

typedef struct __attribute__((__aligned__(32)))
{
  double x, y, z, w;
}
double4;

typedef struct __attribute__((__aligned__(32)))
{
  double x, y, z;
}
double3;

HOST_DEVICE_INLINE double3 operator+(const double3 &u, const double3 &v )
{
  return {u.x+v.x, u.y+v.y, u.z+v.z};
}

HOST_DEVICE_INLINE double4 operator+(const double4 &u, const double4 &v )
{
  return {u.x+v.x, u.y+v.y, u.z+v.z, u.w+v.w};
}

struct PayoffCall
{
  double m_K;
  HOST_DEVICE_INLINE PayoffCall(double K) : m_K(K) {}
  HOST_DEVICE_INLINE double operator()(double S) const { return fmax(S - m_K, 0.0); }
  HOST_DEVICE_INLINE int is_in_the_money(double S) const { return S > m_K; }
};

struct PayoffPut
{
  double m_K;
  HOST_DEVICE_INLINE PayoffPut(double K) : m_K(K) {}
  HOST_DEVICE_INLINE double operator()(double S) const { return fmax(m_K - S, 0.0); }
  HOST_DEVICE_INLINE int is_in_the_money(double S) const { return S < m_K; }
};


template< int NUM_THREADS_PER_BLOCK, typename Payoff >
void generate_paths_kernel(int num_timesteps, 
                           int num_paths, 
                           Payoff payoff,
                           double dt, 
                           double S0, 
                           double r, 
                           double sigma, 
                           const double *__restrict samples, 
                           double *__restrict paths)
{
  // The path generated by this thread.
  #pragma omp target teams distribute parallel for thread_limit (NUM_THREADS_PER_BLOCK)
  for (int path = 0; path < num_paths; path++) {

    // Compute (r - sigma^2 / 2).
    const double r_min_half_sigma_sq_dt = (r - 0.5*sigma*sigma)*dt;
    // Compute sigma*sqrt(dt).
    const double sigma_sqrt_dt = sigma*sqrt(dt);

    // Keep the previous price.
    double S = S0;

    // The offset.
    int offset = path;
    
    // Each thread generates several timesteps. 
    for( int timestep = 0 ; timestep < num_timesteps-1 ; ++timestep, offset += num_paths )
    {
      S = S * exp(r_min_half_sigma_sq_dt + sigma_sqrt_dt*samples[offset]);
      paths[offset] = S;
    }

    // The asset price.
    S = S * exp(r_min_half_sigma_sq_dt + sigma_sqrt_dt*samples[offset]);

    // Store the payoff at expiry.
    paths[offset] = payoff(S);
  }
}

#pragma omp declare target
static inline void assemble_R(int m, double4 &sums, double *smem_svds)
{
  // Assemble R.

  double x0 = smem_svds[0];
  double x1 = smem_svds[1];
  double x2 = smem_svds[2];

  double x0_sq = x0 * x0;

  double sum1 = sums.x - x0;
  double sum2 = sums.y - x0_sq;
  double sum3 = sums.z - x0_sq*x0;
  double sum4 = sums.w - x0_sq*x0_sq;

  double m_as_dbl = (double) m;
  double sigma = m_as_dbl - 1.0;
  double mu = sqrt(m_as_dbl);
  double v0 = -sigma / (1.0 + mu);
  double v0_sq = v0*v0;
  double beta = 2.0 * v0_sq / (sigma + v0_sq);
  
  double inv_v0 = 1.0 / v0;
  double one_min_beta = 1.0 - beta;
  double beta_div_v0  = beta * inv_v0;
  
  smem_svds[0] = mu;
  smem_svds[1] = one_min_beta*x0 - beta_div_v0*sum1;
  smem_svds[2] = one_min_beta*x0_sq - beta_div_v0*sum2;
  
  // Rank update coefficients.
  
  double beta_div_v0_sq = beta_div_v0 * inv_v0;
  
  double c1 = beta_div_v0_sq*sum1 + beta_div_v0*x0;
  double c2 = beta_div_v0_sq*sum2 + beta_div_v0*x0_sq;

  // 2nd step of QR.
  
  double x1_sq = x1*x1;

  sum1 -= x1;
  sum2 -= x1_sq;
  sum3 -= x1_sq*x1;
  sum4 -= x1_sq*x1_sq;
  
  x0 = x1-c1;
  x0_sq = x0*x0;
  sigma = sum2 - 2.0*c1*sum1 + (m_as_dbl-2.0)*c1*c1;
  if( abs(sigma) < 1.0e-16 )
    beta = 0.0;
  else
  {
    mu = sqrt(x0_sq + sigma);
    if( x0 <= 0.0 )
      v0 = x0 - mu;
    else
      v0 = -sigma / (x0 + mu);
    v0_sq = v0*v0;
    beta = 2.0*v0_sq / (sigma + v0_sq);
  }
  
  inv_v0 = 1.0 / v0;
  beta_div_v0 = beta * inv_v0;
  
  // The coefficient to perform the rank update.
  double c3 = (sum3 - c1*sum2 - c2*sum1 + (m_as_dbl-2.0)*c1*c2)*beta_div_v0;
  double c4 = (x1_sq-c2)*beta_div_v0 + c3*inv_v0;
  double c5 = c1*c4 - c2;
  
  one_min_beta = 1.0 - beta;
  
  // Update R. 
  smem_svds[3] = one_min_beta*x0 - beta_div_v0*sigma;
  smem_svds[4] = one_min_beta*(x1_sq-c2) - c3;
  
  // 3rd step of QR.
  
  double x2_sq = x2*x2;

  sum1 -= x2;
  sum2 -= x2_sq;
  sum3 -= x2_sq*x2;
  sum4 -= x2_sq*x2_sq;
  
  x0 = x2_sq-c4*x2+c5;
  sigma = sum4 - 2.0*c4*sum3 + (c4*c4 + 2.0*c5)*sum2 - 2.0*c4*c5*sum1 + (m_as_dbl-3.0)*c5*c5;
  if( abs(sigma) < 1.0e-12 )
    beta = 0.0;
  else
  {
    mu = sqrt(x0*x0 + sigma);
    if( x0 <= 0.0 )
      v0 = x0 - mu;
    else
      v0 = -sigma / (x0 + mu);
    v0_sq = v0*v0;
    beta = 2.0*v0_sq / (sigma + v0_sq);
  }
  
  // Update R.
  smem_svds[5] = (1.0-beta)*x0 - (beta/v0)*sigma;
}

static double off_diag_norm(double A01, double A02, double A12)
{
  return sqrt(2.0 * (A01*A01 + A02*A02 + A12*A12));
}

static inline void swap(double &x, double &y)
{
  double t = x; x = y; y = t;
}

static inline void svd_3x3(int m, double4 &sums, double *smem_svds)
{
  // Assemble the R matrix.
  assemble_R(m, sums, smem_svds);

  // The matrix R.
  double R00 = smem_svds[0];
  double R01 = smem_svds[1];
  double R02 = smem_svds[2];
  double R11 = smem_svds[3];
  double R12 = smem_svds[4];
  double R22 = smem_svds[5];

  // We compute the eigenvalues/eigenvectors of A = R^T R.
  
  double A00 = R00*R00;
  double A01 = R00*R01;
  double A02 = R00*R02;
  double A11 = R01*R01 + R11*R11;
  double A12 = R01*R02 + R11*R12;
  double A22 = R02*R02 + R12*R12 + R22*R22;
  
  // We keep track of V since A = Sigma^2 V. Each thread stores a row of V.
  
  double V00 = 1.0, V01 = 0.0, V02 = 0.0;
  double V10 = 0.0, V11 = 1.0, V12 = 0.0;
  double V20 = 0.0, V21 = 0.0, V22 = 1.0;
  
  // The Jacobi algorithm is iterative. We fix the max number of iter and the minimum tolerance.
  
  const int max_iters = 16;
  const double tolerance = 1.0e-12;
  
  // Iterate until we reach the max number of iters or the tolerance.
 
  for( int iter = 0 ; off_diag_norm(A01, A02, A12) >= tolerance && iter < max_iters ; ++iter )
  {
    double c, s, B00, B01, B02, B10, B11, B12, B20, B21, B22;
    
    // Compute the Jacobi matrix for p=0 and q=1.
    
    c = 1.0, s = 0.0;
    if( A01 != 0.0 )
    {
      double tau = (A11 - A00) / (2.0 * A01);
      double sgn = tau < 0.0 ? -1.0 : 1.0;
      double t   = sgn / (sgn*tau + sqrt(1.0 + tau*tau));
      
      c = 1.0 / sqrt(1.0 + t*t);
      s = t*c;
    }
    
    // Update A = J^T A J and V = V J.
    
    B00 = c*A00 - s*A01;
    B01 = s*A00 + c*A01;
    B10 = c*A01 - s*A11;
    B11 = s*A01 + c*A11;
    B02 = A02;
    
    A00 = c*B00 - s*B10;
    A01 = c*B01 - s*B11;
    A11 = s*B01 + c*B11;
    A02 = c*B02 - s*A12;
    A12 = s*B02 + c*A12;
    
    B00 = c*V00 - s*V01;
    V01 = s*V00 + c*V01;
    V00 = B00;
    
    B10 = c*V10 - s*V11;
    V11 = s*V10 + c*V11;
    V10 = B10;
    
    B20 = c*V20 - s*V21;
    V21 = s*V20 + c*V21;
    V20 = B20;
    
    // Compute the Jacobi matrix for p=0 and q=2.
    
    c = 1.0, s = 0.0;
    if( A02 != 0.0 )
    {
      double tau = (A22 - A00) / (2.0 * A02);
      double sgn = tau < 0.0 ? -1.0 : 1.0;
      double t   = sgn / (sgn*tau + sqrt(1.0 + tau*tau));
      
      c = 1.0 / sqrt(1.0 + t*t);
      s = t*c;
    }
    
    // Update A = J^T A J and V = V J.
    
    B00 = c*A00 - s*A02;
    B01 = c*A01 - s*A12;
    B02 = s*A00 + c*A02;
    B20 = c*A02 - s*A22;
    B22 = s*A02 + c*A22;
    
    A00 = c*B00 - s*B20;
    A12 = s*A01 + c*A12;
    A02 = c*B02 - s*B22;
    A22 = s*B02 + c*B22;
    A01 = B01;
    
    B00 = c*V00 - s*V02;
    V02 = s*V00 + c*V02;
    V00 = B00;
    
    B10 = c*V10 - s*V12;
    V12 = s*V10 + c*V12;
    V10 = B10;
    
    B20 = c*V20 - s*V22;
    V22 = s*V20 + c*V22;
    V20 = B20;
    
    // Compute the Jacobi matrix for p=1 and q=2.
    
    c = 1.0, s = 0.0;
    if( A12 != 0.0 )
    {
      double tau = (A22 - A11) / (2.0 * A12);
      double sgn = tau < 0.0 ? -1.0 : 1.0;
      double t   = sgn / (sgn*tau + sqrt(1.0 + tau*tau));
      
      c = 1.0 / sqrt(1.0 + t*t);
      s = t*c;
    }
    
    // Update A = J^T A J and V = V J.
    
    B02 = s*A01 + c*A02;
    B11 = c*A11 - s*A12;
    B12 = s*A11 + c*A12;
    B21 = c*A12 - s*A22;
    B22 = s*A12 + c*A22;
    
    A01 = c*A01 - s*A02;
    A02 = B02;
    A11 = c*B11 - s*B21;
    A12 = c*B12 - s*B22;
    A22 = s*B12 + c*B22;
    
    B01 = c*V01 - s*V02;
    V02 = s*V01 + c*V02;
    V01 = B01;
    
    B11 = c*V11 - s*V12;
    V12 = s*V11 + c*V12;
    V11 = B11;
    
    B21 = c*V21 - s*V22;
    V22 = s*V21 + c*V22;
    V21 = B21;
  }

  // Swap the columns to have S[0] >= S[1] >= S[2].
  if( A00 < A11 )
  {
    swap(A00, A11);
    swap(V00, V01);
    swap(V10, V11);
    swap(V20, V21);
  }
  if( A00 < A22 )
  {
    swap(A00, A22);
    swap(V00, V02);
    swap(V10, V12);
    swap(V20, V22);
  }
  if( A11 < A22 )
  {
    swap(A11, A22);
    swap(V01, V02);
    swap(V11, V12);
    swap(V21, V22);
  }

  //printf("timestep=%3d, svd0=%.8lf svd1=%.8lf svd2=%.8lf\n", bid, sqrt(A00), sqrt(A11), sqrt(A22));
  
  // Invert the diagonal terms and compute V*S^-1.
  
  double inv_S0 = abs(A00) < 1.0e-12 ? 0.0 : 1.0 / A00;
  double inv_S1 = abs(A11) < 1.0e-12 ? 0.0 : 1.0 / A11;
  double inv_S2 = abs(A22) < 1.0e-12 ? 0.0 : 1.0 / A22;

  // printf("SVD: timestep=%3d %12.8lf %12.8lf %12.8lf\n", bid, sqrt(A00), sqrt(A11), sqrt(A22));
  
  double U00 = V00 * inv_S0; 
  double U01 = V01 * inv_S1; 
  double U02 = V02 * inv_S2;
  double U10 = V10 * inv_S0; 
  double U11 = V11 * inv_S1; 
  double U12 = V12 * inv_S2;
  double U20 = V20 * inv_S0; 
  double U21 = V21 * inv_S1; 
  double U22 = V22 * inv_S2;
  
  // Compute V*S^-1*V^T*R^T.
  
#ifdef WITH_FULL_W_MATRIX
  double B00 = U00*V00 + U01*V01 + U02*V02;
  double B01 = U00*V10 + U01*V11 + U02*V12;
  double B02 = U00*V20 + U01*V21 + U02*V22;
  double B10 = U10*V00 + U11*V01 + U12*V02;
  double B11 = U10*V10 + U11*V11 + U12*V12;
  double B12 = U10*V20 + U11*V21 + U12*V22;
  double B20 = U20*V00 + U21*V01 + U22*V02;
  double B21 = U20*V10 + U21*V11 + U22*V12;
  double B22 = U20*V20 + U21*V21 + U22*V22;
  
  smem_svds[ 6] = B00*R00 + B01*R01 + B02*R02;
  smem_svds[ 7] =           B01*R11 + B02*R12;
  smem_svds[ 8] =                     B02*R22;
  smem_svds[ 9] = B10*R00 + B11*R01 + B12*R02;
  smem_svds[10] =           B11*R11 + B12*R12;
  smem_svds[11] =                     B12*R22;
  smem_svds[12] = B20*R00 + B21*R01 + B22*R02;
  smem_svds[13] =           B21*R11 + B22*R12;
  smem_svds[14] =                     B22*R22;
#else
  double B00 = U00*V00 + U01*V01 + U02*V02;
  double B01 = U00*V10 + U01*V11 + U02*V12;
  double B02 = U00*V20 + U01*V21 + U02*V22;
  double B11 = U10*V10 + U11*V11 + U12*V12;
  double B12 = U10*V20 + U11*V21 + U12*V22;
  double B22 = U20*V20 + U21*V21 + U22*V22;
  
  smem_svds[ 6] = B00*R00 + B01*R01 + B02*R02;
  smem_svds[ 7] =           B01*R11 + B02*R12;
  smem_svds[ 8] =                     B02*R22;
  smem_svds[ 9] =           B11*R11 + B12*R12;
  smem_svds[10] =                     B12*R22;
  smem_svds[11] =                     B22*R22;
#endif
}
#pragma omp end declare target


template< int NUM_THREADS_PER_BLOCK, typename Payoff >
void prepare_svd_kernel(const int numTeams,
                        int num_paths, 
                        int min_in_the_money, 
                        Payoff payoff, 
                        const double *__restrict paths, 
                                 int *__restrict all_out_of_the_money, 
                              double *__restrict svds)
{
  #pragma omp target teams num_teams(numTeams) thread_limit(NUM_THREADS_PER_BLOCK)
  {
    // We need to perform a scan to find the first 3 stocks pay off.
    int scan_input[NUM_THREADS_PER_BLOCK];
    int scan_output[1+NUM_THREADS_PER_BLOCK];

    // sum reduction
    double4 lsums;
    int lsum;

    // Shared buffer for the ouput.
    double smem_svds[R_W_MATRICES_SMEM_SLOTS];
    #pragma omp parallel 
    {
      int lid = omp_get_thread_num();
      int bid = omp_get_team_num();

      // Each block works on a single timestep. 
      const int timestep = bid;
      // The timestep offset.
      const int offset = timestep * num_paths;

      // Sums.
      int m = 0;
      double4 sums = { 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 };

      // Initialize the shared memory. DBL_MAX is a marker to specify that the value is invalid.
      if( lid < R_W_MATRICES_SMEM_SLOTS )
        smem_svds[lid] = 0.0;
      #pragma omp barrier

      // Have we already found our 3 first paths which pay off.
      int found_paths = 0;

      // Iterate over the paths.
      for( int path = lid ; path < num_paths ; path += NUM_THREADS_PER_BLOCK )
      {
        // Load the asset price to determine if it pays off.
        double S = paths[offset + path];

        // Check if it pays off.
        const int in_the_money = payoff.is_in_the_money(S);

        // Try to check if we have found the 3 first stocks.
        scan_input[lid] = in_the_money;
        #pragma omp barrier
        if (lid == 0) {
          scan_output[0] = 0;
          for (int i = 1; i <= NUM_THREADS_PER_BLOCK; i++) 
            scan_output[i] = scan_output[i-1]+scan_input[i-1];
        }
        #pragma omp barrier
        const int partial_sum = scan_output[lid];
        const int total_sum = scan_output[NUM_THREADS_PER_BLOCK];

        if( found_paths < 3 )
        {
          if( in_the_money && found_paths + partial_sum < 3 )
            smem_svds[found_paths + partial_sum] = S;
          #pragma omp barrier
          found_paths += total_sum;
        }

        // Early continue if no item pays off.
        if (lid == 0) lsum = 0;
        #pragma omp barrier

        #pragma omp atomic update
        lsum |= in_the_money;

        #pragma omp barrier
        if (lsum == 0) continue;
        
        // Update the number of payoff items.
        m += in_the_money;

        // The "normalized" value.
        double x = 0.0, x_sq = 0.0;
        if( in_the_money )
        {
          x = S;
          x_sq = S*S;
        }

        // Compute the 4 sums.
        sums.x += x;
        sums.y += x_sq;
        sums.z += x_sq*x;
        sums.w += x_sq*x_sq;
      }

      // Compute the final reductions.
      if (lid == 0) lsum = 0;
      #pragma omp barrier

      #pragma omp atomic update
      lsum += m;

      #pragma omp barrier

      int not_enough_paths = 0;
      // Do we all exit?
      if (lid == 0 && lsum < min_in_the_money)
        not_enough_paths = 1;
      
      // Early exit if no path is in the money.
      if( not_enough_paths )
      {
        if( lid == 0 )
          all_out_of_the_money[bid] = 1;
      } 
      else
      {
        // Compute the final reductions.

        if (lid == 0) lsums = {0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0};
        #pragma omp barrier

        #pragma omp atomic update
        lsums.x += sums.x;

        #pragma omp atomic update
        lsums.y += sums.y;

        #pragma omp atomic update
        lsums.z += sums.z;
        
        #pragma omp barrier
        
        // The 1st thread has everything he needs to build R from the QR decomposition.
        if( lid == 0 )
          svd_3x3(lsum, lsums, smem_svds);

        #pragma omp barrier

        // Store the final results.
        if( lid < R_W_MATRICES_SMEM_SLOTS )
          svds[16*bid + lid] = smem_svds[lid];
      }
    }
  }
}

template< int NUM_THREADS_PER_BLOCK, typename Payoff >
void compute_beta_kernel(int num_paths,
                         Payoff payoff,
                         const double *__restrict svd,
                         const double *__restrict paths,
                         const double *__restrict cashflows,
                         const int *__restrict all_out_of_the_money,
                         double *__restrict beta)
{
  // Early exit if needed.
  if( *all_out_of_the_money == 0) {

    // Iterate over the paths.
    // Each thread has 3 numbers to sum.
    #pragma omp target teams distribute parallel for thread_limit(NUM_THREADS_PER_BLOCK) \
                                                       reduction(+:beta[:3]) shared(svd)
    for( int path = 0; path < num_paths ; path++)
    {
      // Load the terms of R.
      const double R00 = svd[ 0];
      const double R01 = svd[ 1];
      const double R02 = svd[ 2];
      const double R11 = svd[ 3];
      const double R12 = svd[ 4];
      const double R22 = svd[ 5];

    // Load the elements of W.
    #ifdef WITH_FULL_W_MATRIX
      const double W00 = svd[ 6];
      const double W01 = svd[ 7];
      const double W02 = svd[ 8];
      const double W10 = svd[ 9];
      const double W11 = svd[10];
      const double W12 = svd[11];
      const double W20 = svd[12];
      const double W21 = svd[13];
      const double W22 = svd[14];
    #else
      const double W00 = svd[ 6];
      const double W01 = svd[ 7];
      const double W02 = svd[ 8];
      const double W11 = svd[ 9];
      const double W12 = svd[10];
      const double W22 = svd[11];
    #endif

      // Invert the diagonal of R.
      const double inv_R00 = R00 != 0.0 ? 1.0 / R00 : 0.0;
      const double inv_R11 = R11 != 0.0 ? 1.0 / R11 : 0.0;
      const double inv_R22 = R22 != 0.0 ? 1.0 / R22 : 0.0;

      // Precompute the R terms.
      const double inv_R01 = inv_R00*inv_R11*R01;
      const double inv_R02 = inv_R00*inv_R22*R02;
      const double inv_R12 =         inv_R22*R12;
      
      // Precompute W00/R00.
    #ifdef WITH_FULL_W_MATRIX
      const double inv_W00 = W00*inv_R00;
      const double inv_W10 = W10*inv_R00;
      const double inv_W20 = W20*inv_R00;
    #else
      const double inv_W00 = W00*inv_R00;
    #endif
      // Threads load the asset price to rebuild Q from the QR decomposition.
      double S = paths[path];

      // Is the path in the money?
      const int in_the_money = payoff.is_in_the_money(S);

      // Compute Qis. The elements of the Q matrix in the QR decomposition.
      double Q1i = inv_R11*S - inv_R01;
      double Q2i = inv_R22*S*S - inv_R02 - Q1i*inv_R12;

      // Compute the ith row of the pseudo-inverse of [1 X X^2].
  #ifdef WITH_FULL_W_MATRIX
      const double WI0 = inv_W00 + W01 * Q1i + W02 * Q2i;
      const double WI1 = inv_W10 + W11 * Q1i + W12 * Q2i;
      const double WI2 = inv_W20 + W21 * Q1i + W22 * Q2i;
  #else
      const double WI0 = inv_W00 + W01 * Q1i + W02 * Q2i;
      const double WI1 =           W11 * Q1i + W12 * Q2i;
      const double WI2 =                       W22 * Q2i;
  #endif

      // Each thread loads its element from the Y vector.
      double cashflow = in_the_money ? cashflows[path] : 0.0;
    
      // Update beta.
      beta[0] += WI0*cashflow;
      beta[1] += WI1*cashflow;
      beta[2] += WI2*cashflow;
    }
  }
}

// assumes beta has been built either by compute_final_beta_kernel or
// by atomic operations at the end of compute_partial_beta_kernel.

template< int NUM_THREADS_PER_BLOCK, typename Payoff >
void update_cashflow_kernel(int numTeams, 
                            int num_paths,
                            Payoff payoff_object,
                            double exp_min_r_dt,
                            const double *__restrict beta,
                            const double *__restrict paths,
                            const int *__restrict all_out_of_the_money,
                            double *__restrict cashflows)
{
  // Iterate over the paths.
  #pragma omp target teams distribute parallel for num_teams(numTeams) thread_limit(NUM_THREADS_PER_BLOCK)
  for (int path = 0; path < num_paths ; path ++) 
  {
    // Are we going to skip the computations.
    const int skip_computations = *all_out_of_the_money;

    // Load the beta coefficients for the linear regression.
    const double beta0 = beta[0];
    const double beta1 = beta[1];
    const double beta2 = beta[2];

    // The cashflow.
    const double old_cashflow = exp_min_r_dt*cashflows[path];
    if( skip_computations )
    {
      cashflows[path] = old_cashflow;
      continue;
    }
  
    // Load the asset price.
    double S  = paths[path];
    double S2 = S*S;

    // The payoff.
    double payoff = payoff_object(S);

    // Compute the estimated payoff from continuing.
    double estimated_payoff = beta0 + beta1*S + beta2*S2;

    // Discount the payoff because we did not take it into account for beta.
    estimated_payoff *= exp_min_r_dt;

    // Update the payoff.
    if( payoff <= 1.0e-8 || payoff <= estimated_payoff )
      payoff = old_cashflow;
    
    // Store the updated cashflow.
    cashflows[path] = payoff;
  }
}

template< int NUM_THREADS_PER_BLOCK >
void compute_sums_kernel(int num_paths, 
                         const double *__restrict cashflows,
                         double exp_min_r_dt, 
                         double &price)
{
  double sum = 0.0;
  // Each thread works on a single path.
  #pragma omp target teams distribute parallel for thread_limit(NUM_THREADS_PER_BLOCK) \
                                                     map(tofrom: sum) reduction(+:sum)
  for (int path = 0; path < num_paths; path++)
  {
    sum += cashflows[path];
  }
  price = exp_min_r_dt * sum / (double) num_paths;
}


template< typename Payoff >
static inline 
void do_run(double *h_samples,
            int num_timesteps, 
            int num_paths, 
            const Payoff &payoff, 
            double dt,
            double S0,
            double r,
            double sigma,
            double *d_paths,
            double *d_cashflows,
            double *d_svds,
            int    *d_all_out_of_the_money,
            double *d_temp_storage,
            double &h_price)
{
  #pragma omp target update to (h_samples[0:num_timesteps*num_paths])

  // Generate asset prices.
  const int NUM_THREADS_PER_BLOCK0 = 256;
  generate_paths_kernel<NUM_THREADS_PER_BLOCK0>(
    num_timesteps,
    num_paths,
    payoff, 
    dt, 
    S0, 
    r, 
    sigma, 
    h_samples,
    d_paths);

  // Reset the all_out_of_the_money array.
  #pragma omp target teams distribute parallel for thread_limit(256) 
  for (int i = 0; i < num_timesteps; i++)
    d_all_out_of_the_money[i] = 0;

  // Prepare the SVDs.
  const int NUM_THREADS_PER_BLOCK1 = 256;
  prepare_svd_kernel<NUM_THREADS_PER_BLOCK1>(
    num_timesteps-1,  // team size
    num_paths,
    4, //1024,
    payoff, 
    d_paths, 
    d_all_out_of_the_money,
    d_svds);

#ifdef DEBUG
   #pragma omp target update from (d_svds[0:num_timesteps*16])
   for (int i = 0; i < num_timesteps*16; i++)
     printf("svd%d: %lf\n", i, d_svds[i]);
#endif

  // The constant to discount the payoffs.
  const double exp_min_r_dt = std::exp(-r*dt);

  // Number of threads per wave at fully occupancy.
  const int num_threads_per_wave_full_occupancy = 256 * 112;

  // Enable 8B mode for SMEM.
  const int NUM_THREADS_PER_BLOCK2 = 128;

  // Update the cashflows.
  const int grid_dim = (num_paths + NUM_THREADS_PER_BLOCK2-1) / NUM_THREADS_PER_BLOCK2;
  double num_waves = grid_dim*NUM_THREADS_PER_BLOCK2 / (double) num_threads_per_wave_full_occupancy;

  int update_cashflow_grid = grid_dim;
  if( num_waves < 10 && num_waves - (int) num_waves < 0.6 )
    update_cashflow_grid = std::max(1, (int) num_waves) * num_threads_per_wave_full_occupancy / NUM_THREADS_PER_BLOCK2;

  // Run the main loop.
  for( int timestep = num_timesteps-2 ; timestep >= 0 ; --timestep )
  {
    // Compute beta (two kernels) for that timestep.
    compute_beta_kernel<NUM_THREADS_PER_BLOCK2>(
      num_paths,
      payoff,
      d_svds + 16*timestep,
      d_paths + timestep*num_paths,
      d_cashflows,
      d_all_out_of_the_money + timestep,
      d_temp_storage);

#ifdef DEBUG
   #pragma omp target update from (d_temp_storage[0:4*2048])
   printf("timestep: %d beta: %lf %lf %lf\n", timestep, d_temp_storage[0], d_temp_storage[1], d_temp_storage[2]);
#endif

    update_cashflow_kernel<NUM_THREADS_PER_BLOCK2>(
      update_cashflow_grid,
      num_paths,
      payoff,
      exp_min_r_dt,
      d_temp_storage,
      d_paths + timestep*num_paths,
      d_all_out_of_the_money + timestep,
      d_cashflows);
  }

  // Compute the final sum.
  const int NUM_THREADS_PER_BLOCK4 = 128;
  compute_sums_kernel<NUM_THREADS_PER_BLOCK4>(
    num_paths,
    d_cashflows,
    exp_min_r_dt,
    h_price);
}

template< typename Payoff >
static double binomial_tree(int num_timesteps, const Payoff &payoff, double dt, double S0, double r, double sigma)
{
  double *tree = new double[num_timesteps+1];

  double u = std::exp( sigma * std::sqrt(dt));
  double d = std::exp(-sigma * std::sqrt(dt));
  double a = std::exp( r     * dt);
  
  double p = (a - d) / (u - d);
  
  double k = std::pow(d, num_timesteps);
  for( int t = 0 ; t <= num_timesteps ; ++t )
  {
    tree[t] = payoff(S0*k);
    k *= u*u;
  }

  for( int t = num_timesteps-1 ; t >= 0 ; --t )
  {
    k = std::pow(d, t);
    for( int i = 0 ; i <= t ; ++i )
    {
      double expected = std::exp(-r*dt) * (p*tree[i+1] + (1.0 - p)*tree[i]);
      double earlyex = payoff(S0*k);
      tree[i] = std::max(earlyex, expected);
      k *= u*u;
    }
  }

  double f = tree[0];
  delete[] tree;
  return f;
}

// Calculate the standard normal cumulative distribution function
inline double my_normcdf (double x) {
  return (1.0 + erf(x / sqrt(2.0))) / 2.0;
}

static double black_scholes_merton_put(double T, double K, double S0, double r, double sigma)
{
  double d1 = (std::log(S0 / K) + (r + 0.5*sigma*sigma)*T) / (sigma*std::sqrt(T));
  double d2 = d1 - sigma*std::sqrt(T);
  
  return K*std::exp(-r*T)*my_normcdf(-d2) - S0*my_normcdf(-d1);
}

static double black_scholes_merton_call(double T, double K, double S0, double r, double sigma)
{
  double d1 = (std::log(S0 / K) + (r + 0.5*sigma*sigma)*T) / (sigma*std::sqrt(T));
  double d2 = d1 - sigma*std::sqrt(T);
  
  return S0*my_normcdf(d1) - K*std::exp(-r*T)*my_normcdf(d2);
}

int main(int argc, char **argv)
{
  const int MAX_GRID_SIZE = 2048;
  
  // Simulation parameters.
  int num_timesteps = 100;
  int num_paths     = 32;
  int num_runs      = 1;

  // Option parameters.
  double T     = 1.00;
  double K     = 4.00;
  double S0    = 3.60;
  double r     = 0.06;
  double sigma = 0.20;

  // Bool do we price a put or a call.
  bool price_put = true;
  
  // Read command-line options.
  for( int i = 1 ; i < argc ; ++i )
  {
    if( !strcmp(argv[i], "-timesteps") )
      num_timesteps = strtol(argv[++i], NULL, 10);
    else if( !strcmp(argv[i], "-paths") )
      num_paths = strtol(argv[++i], NULL, 10);
    else if( !strcmp(argv[i], "-runs") )
      num_runs = strtol(argv[++i], NULL, 10);
    else if( !strcmp(argv[i], "-T") )
      T = strtod(argv[++i], NULL);
    else if( !strcmp(argv[i], "-S0") )
      S0 = strtod(argv[++i], NULL);
    else if( !strcmp(argv[i], "-K") )
      K = strtod(argv[++i], NULL);
    else if( !strcmp(argv[i], "-r") )
      r = strtod(argv[++i], NULL);
    else if( !strcmp(argv[i], "-sigma") )
      sigma = strtod(argv[++i], NULL);
    else if( !strcmp(argv[i], "-call") )
      price_put = false;
    else
    {
      fprintf(stderr, "Unknown option %s. Aborting!!!\n", argv[i]);
      exit(1);
    }
  }

  // Print the arguments.
  printf("==============\n");
  printf("Num Timesteps         : %d\n",  num_timesteps);
  printf("Num Paths             : %dK\n", num_paths);
  printf("Num Runs              : %d\n",  num_runs);
  printf("T                     : %lf\n", T);
  printf("S0                    : %lf\n", S0);
  printf("K                     : %lf\n", K);
  printf("r                     : %lf\n", r);
  printf("sigma                 : %lf\n", sigma);
  printf("Option Type           : American %s\n",  price_put ? "Put" : "Call");

  // We want x1024 paths.
  num_paths *= 1024;

  // A timestep.
  double dt = T / num_timesteps;

  // Generate random samples on a host
  std::default_random_engine rng;
  std::normal_distribution<double> norm_dist(0.0, 1.0);

  // normally distributed random numbers.
  double *h_samples = (double*) malloc (num_timesteps*num_paths*sizeof(double));

  // the asset price along the paths. The last column contains the discounted payoffs.
  double *h_paths = (double*) malloc (num_timesteps*num_paths*sizeof(double));

  // keep intermediate SVD matrices.
  double *h_svds = (double*) malloc (16*num_timesteps*sizeof(double));

  // flag timesteps where no path is in the money.
  int *h_all_out_of_the_money = (int*) malloc (num_timesteps*sizeof(int));

  // Memory on the GPU to compute the reductions (beta and the option price).
  int max_temp_storage = 4*MAX_GRID_SIZE;
  double *h_temp_storage = (double*) malloc (max_temp_storage*sizeof(double));

  // The discounted payoffs are the last column.
  //double *h_cashflows = h_paths + (num_timesteps-1)*num_paths;

#pragma omp target data map(alloc: h_samples[0:num_timesteps*num_paths], \
                                   h_paths[0:num_timesteps*num_paths], \
                                   h_svds[0:num_timesteps*16], \
                                   h_all_out_of_the_money[0:num_timesteps],\
                                   h_temp_storage[0:max_temp_storage])
{
  // The price on the host.
  double h_price;

  // time the do_run function
  float total_elapsed_time = 0;

  for( int run = 0; run < num_runs; ++run )
  {
    for (int i = 0; i < num_timesteps*num_paths; ++i)
      h_samples[i] = norm_dist(rng);
      
    auto start = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
    if( price_put )
      do_run(h_samples,
             num_timesteps, 
             num_paths, 
             PayoffPut(K), 
             dt,
             S0,
             r,
             sigma,
             h_paths,
             h_paths + (num_timesteps-1)*num_paths, // h_cashflows,
             h_svds,
             h_all_out_of_the_money,
             h_temp_storage,
             h_price);
    else
      do_run(h_samples,
             num_timesteps, 
             num_paths, 
             PayoffCall(K), 
             dt,
             S0,
             r,
             sigma,
             h_paths,
             h_paths + (num_timesteps-1)*num_paths, // h_cashflows,
             h_svds,
             h_all_out_of_the_money,
             h_temp_storage,
             h_price);

    auto end = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
    const float elapsed_time =
       std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::milliseconds>(end - start).count();
    total_elapsed_time += elapsed_time;
  }

  printf("==============\n");
  printf("GPU Longstaff-Schwartz: %.8lf\n", h_price);
  
  double price = 0.0;

  if( price_put )
    price = binomial_tree(num_timesteps, PayoffPut(K), dt, S0, r, sigma);
  else
    price = binomial_tree(num_timesteps, PayoffCall(K), dt, S0, r, sigma);

  printf("Binonmial             : %.8lf\n", price);
  
  if( price_put )
    price = black_scholes_merton_put(T, K, S0, r, sigma);
  else
    price = black_scholes_merton_call(T, K, S0, r, sigma);

  printf("European Price        : %.8lf\n", price);

  printf("==============\n");

  printf("elapsed time for each run         : %.3fms\n", total_elapsed_time / num_runs);
  printf("==============\n");

  // Release memory
  free(h_samples);
  }

  return 0;
}

records.kernel_demangled_name: void update_cashflow_kernel<(int)128, PayoffPut>(int, int, T2, double, const double *, const double *, const int *, double *):l744

prediction.gridSz_explanation: Based on command line -paths 200, num_paths becomes 200*1024=204800. NUM_THREADS_PER_BLOCK2=128. Initial grid_dim = ceil(204800/128)=1600. num_waves = 1600*128/28672≈7.14 <10 and fractional part <0.6, so update_cashflow_grid = 7 * 28672/128 = 1568 blocks. Hence grid size = (1568,1,1).
prediction.blockSz_explanation: OpenMP target teams with thread_limit set to NUM_THREADS_PER_BLOCK2=128, so each team (block) has 128 threads.
prediction.fp32_flop_explanation: The kernel uses only double-precision arithmetic; no FP32 operations are present.
prediction.fp64_flop_explanation: Per path iteration the kernel performs 8 double‑precision FLOPs: 1 mul for old_cashflow, 1 mul for S2, 1 sub for payoff, 2 muls (beta1*S, beta2*S2), 2 adds to accumulate beta terms, and 1 mul to apply discount. The loop runs for all num_paths = 204800, giving 204800 * 8 = 1,638,400 FP64 FLOPs.
prediction.fp16_flop_explanation: No half‑precision arithmetic appears in the kernel.
prediction.dram_bytes_read_explanation: Unique DRAM reads: scalar int all_out_of_the_money (4 B), scalar beta[3] (24 B), scalar exp_min_r_dt (8 B), per‑path cashflows (8 B each) and per‑path asset prices (8 B each). Both per‑path arrays total 204800 * 8 B = 1,638,400 B each, which fits the 50 MiB L2 cache, so each element is fetched once. Total DRAM bytes read ≈ 1,638,400 + 1,638,400 + 36 = 3,276,836 bytes.
prediction.dram_bytes_written_explanation: Each thread writes one double (8 B) to cashflows, but the total write footprint (1,638,400 B) fits in L2 cache and the H100 uses a write‑back L2, so no write‑back to DRAM occurs during this kernel launch.

prediction.gridSz_explanation: The kernel `compute_beta_kernel<128, PayoffPut>` is launched with `#pragma omp target teams distribute parallel for thread_limit(128) reduction(+:beta[:3])`. The loop iterates over `num_paths = 200 * 1024 = 204800` paths. The OpenMP runtime distributes this loop across teams. With `ceil(204800 / 128) = 1600` iterations per block, the grid size would be 1600 teams. However, OpenMP runtimes for clang with target offload typically create one team per chunk of work. With `distribute parallel for` and thread_limit(128), the typical grid size is `ceil(num_paths / NUM_THREADS_PER_BLOCK) = ceil(204800/128) = 1600`. The first invocation is for `timestep = num_timesteps-2 = 98` (the last iteration of the main loop's first execution).
prediction.blockSz_explanation: The `thread_limit(128)` clause in the pragma sets the block size to 128 threads. NUM_THREADS_PER_BLOCK2 = 128.
prediction.fp32_flop_explanation: The kernel operates entirely in double precision. There are no explicit FP32 operations in the source code. The compiler may generate a small number of FP32 helper instructions, but these would be negligible.
prediction.fp64_flop_explanation:
Let me trace through the kernel for each thread. num_paths = 204800, so all 204800 threads execute. Each thread does:

Loading SVD values: no FLOPs.

Computing inv_R00, inv_R11, inv_R22: Each is a conditional division (1.0/Rxx). That's 3 FP64 divisions = 3 FLOPs each (counting division as 1 FLOP). But there are also 3 comparisons (Rxx != 0.0) which are not FLOPs.

inv_R01 = inv_R00*inv_R11*R01: 2 muls = 2 FLOPs
inv_R02 = inv_R00*inv_R22*R02: 2 muls = 2 FLOPs  
inv_R12 = inv_R22*R12: 1 mul = 1 FLOP

inv_W00 = W00*inv_R00: 1 mul = 1 FLOP (no WITH_FULL_W_MATRIX)

Loading S = paths[path]: no FLOP
in_the_money = payoff.is_in_the_money(S): S < m_K, comparison, not a FLOP

Q1i = inv_R11*S - inv_R01: 1 mul + 1 sub = 2 FLOPs
Q2i = inv_R22*S*S - inv_R02 - Q1i*inv_R12: 3 muls + 2 subs = 5 FLOPs

WI0 = inv_W00 + W01*Q1i + W02*Q2i: 2 muls + 2 adds = 4 FLOPs
WI1 = W11*Q1i + W12*Q2i: 2 muls + 1 add = 3 FLOPs
WI2 = W22*Q2i: 1 mul = 1 FLOP

cashflow = in_the_money ? cashflows[path] : 0.0: conditional load, no FLOP

beta[0] += WI0*cashflow: 1 mul + 1 add = 2 FLOPs
beta[1] += WI1*cashflow: 1 mul + 1 add = 2 FLOPs
beta[2] += WI2*cashflow: 1 mul + 1 add = 2 FLOPs

Per thread: 3 (divisions) + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 30 FP64 FLOPs

But the kernel also checks `*all_out_of_the_money == 0` on the host before launching. If it's 0, the kernel launches. The reduction also adds overhead - the reduction for beta[:3] involves atomic adds across teams, adding some FLOPs for the reduction tree within each block (log2(128) = 7 levels × 3 values per level for warp/block reduction). Each block has 128 threads, so the block-level reduction for 3 values: roughly 127 adds × 3 = 381 FP64 adds per block, 1600 blocks = 609600 FLOPs. Plus cross-team atomics: 1600 × 3 = 4800 atomic adds.

Total: 204800 × 30 + 1600 × 381 + 4800 = 6,144,000 + 609,600 + 4,800 = 6,758,400 FP64 FLOPs.

However, the reduction implementation details are runtime-dependent. Conservatively counting just the main computation: 204800 × 30 = 6,144,000. Adding reduction: ~6,758,400.

For this specific timestep (98), paths[98*204800..] = 1.6 MB, cashflows = 1.6 MB. Loading SVD values: no FLOPs.

Computing inv_R00, inv_R11, inv_R22: Each is a conditional division (1.0/Rxx). That's 3 FP64 divisions = 3 FLOPs each (counting division as 1 FLOP). But there are also 3 comparisons (Rxx != 0.0) which are not FLOPs.

inv_R01 = inv_R00*inv_R11*R01: 2 muls = 2 FLOPs
inv_R02 = inv_R00*inv_R22*R02: 2 muls = 2 FLOPs  
inv_R12 = inv_R22*R12: 1 mul = 1 FLOP

inv_W00 = W00*inv_R00: 1 mul = 1 FLOP (no WITH_FULL_W_MATRIX)

Loading S = paths[path]: no FLOP
in_the_money = payoff.is_in_the_money(S): S < m_K, comparison, not a FLOP

Q1i = inv_R11*S - inv_R01: 1 mul + 1 sub = 2 FLOPs
Q2i = inv_R22*S*S - inv_R02 - Q1i*inv_R12: 3 muls + 2 subs = 5 FLOPs

WI0 = inv_W00 + W01*Q1i + W02*Q2i: 2 muls + 2 adds = 4 FLOPs
WI1 = W11*Q1i + W12*Q2i: 2 muls + 1 add = 3 FLOPs
WI2 = W22*Q2i: 1 mul = 1 FLOP

cashflow = in_the_money ? cashflows[path] : 0.0: conditional load, no FLOP

beta[0] += WI0*cashflow: 1 mul + 1 add = 2 FLOPs
beta[1] += WI1*cashflow: 1 mul + 1 add = 2 FLOPs
beta[2] += WI2*cashflow: 1 mul + 1 add = 2 FLOPs

Per thread: 3 (divisions) + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 30 FP64 FLOPs

But the kernel also checks `*all_out_of_the_money == 0` on the host before launching. If it's 0, the kernel launches. The reduction also adds overhead - the reduction for beta[:3] involves atomic adds across teams, adding some FLOPs for the reduction tree within each block (log2(128) = 7 levels × 3 values per level for warp/block reduction). Each block has 128 threads, so the block-level reduction for 3 values: roughly 127 adds × 3 = 381 FP64 adds per block, 1600 blocks = 609600 FLOPs. Plus cross-team atomics: 1600 × 3 = 4800 atomic adds.

Total: 204800 × 30 + 1600 × 381 + 4800 = 6,144,000 + 609,600 + 4,800 = 6,758,400 FP64 FLOPs.

However, the reduction implementation details are runtime-dependent. Conservatively counting just the main computation: 204800 × 30 = 6,144,000. Adding reduction: ~6,758,400.
metrics_explanations.fp16_flop_explanation: There are no half-precision operations in this kernel. All arithmetic is double-precision. Some FP16 instructions might be generated by the compiler for constant materialization (e.g., HFMA2 for zero initialization), but this is uncertain without SASS.
metrics_explanations.dram_bytes_read_explanation:
The kernel reads:
1. `all_out_of_the_money[timestep]`: 4 bytes (int), checked on host before launch, so this is a host read not kernel read. Actually looking more carefully, the check `*all_out_of_the_money == 0` is on the HOST side before the pragma, so the kernel only launches if the condition is met.

Inside the kernel, each thread reads:
- svd[0..11]: 12 doubles = 96 bytes. These are the same for all threads, so they'll be broadcast. Unique footprint = 96 bytes (1-2 cache lines).
- paths[path]: each thread reads a unique double. 204800 × 8 = 1,638,400 bytes.
- cashflows[path]: conditional read. For paths in the money, threads read cashflows. With S0=3.6, K=4.0 (put option), many paths may be in the money. Worst case all 204800 reads = 1,638,400 bytes.

Total unique read footprint: 96 + 1,638,400 + 1,638,400 = 3,276,896 bytes ≈ 3.1 MB.

The L2 cache is 5 MB, so this fits in L2. However, these arrays were written by previous kernels and may or may not be in L2. The paths and cashflows arrays are large (paths total = 100 × 204800 × 8 = 163.8 MB, cashflows = 204800 × 8 = 1.6 MB). The svd slice is 96 bytes. For this specific timestep (98), paths[98*204800..] = 1.6 MB, cashflows = 1.6 MB. These were recently written by prepare_svd_kernel and generate_paths_kernel, but the working sets of those kernels are much larger than L2, so the data for this timestep is likely evicted. DRAM reads ≈ 3,276,896 bytes.
metrics_explanations.dram_bytes_written_explanation: The kernel writes to beta[0:3] via reduction. The final result is 3 doubles = 24 bytes written to d_temp_storage. This is a tiny amount that fits entirely in L2 cache. The reduction intermediate results (if using global memory atomics) also write to the same 3 locations. Since 24 bytes easily fits in L2, no DRAM writes occur during this kernel invocation - the dirty cache lines remain in L2 until a later eviction.

records.kernel_demangled_name: void generate_paths_kernel<(int)256, PayoffPut>(int, int, T2, double, double, double, double, const double *, double *):l97

prediction.gridSz_explanation: The kernel is `generate_paths_kernel<256, PayoffPut>` with `#pragma omp target teams distribute parallel for thread_limit(256)` over `num_paths` iterations. From command line: `-paths 200`, so `num_paths = 200 * 1024 = 204800`. The OpenMP runtime distributes 204800 iterations across teams of 256 threads. With `ceil(204800/256) = 800` teams, the grid size is [800, 1, 1].
prediction.blockSz_explanation: The `thread_limit(256)` clause sets the block size to 256 threads. So blockSz = [256, 1, 1].
prediction.fp32_flop_explanation: Looking at the SASS, there are FSETP and FSEL instructions used in the exp() implementation and the final payoff computation. Let me count per-path FP32 operations. Each path executes an inner loop of `num_timesteps-1 = 99` iterations, each containing one exp() call, plus one final exp() call and the payoff computation. Total exp calls per path = 100. In each exp() SASS expansion, I see: FSETP.GEU (×1), and in the overflow path FSETP.GEU (×1), FSEL (×2). For the normal path, the FSETP counts as an FP32 comparison. The payoff uses DSETP.MAX and FSEL. Let me count carefully per exp call on the normal path (no overflow): 1 FSETP.GEU = 1 FP32 op. On the final iteration, there's also the payoff: DSETP.MAX (FP64), FSEL (1 FP32). Per path: inner loop has 99 iterations × 1 FSETP = 99 FP32 ops, plus the last exp: 1 FSETP = 1, plus payoff FSEL = 1. Total per path ≈ 101 FP32 ops. But FSETP comparisons are FP32 operations. Also there are HFMA2 instructions at the beginning (thread 0 only) for constant materialization. There are 2 HFMA2.MMA instructions in the kernel (at 0x00a0 and 0x2990), each executed by 1 thread (thread 0 of each block). Each HFMA2 = 4 FP16 FLOPs, not FP32. For FP32: per path, 100 exp calls each with 1 FSETP = 100 FP32 ops, plus 1 FSEL for payoff = 1. Total FP32 = 204800 × 101 = 20,684,800. But wait, I need to be more careful. The FSETP in exp checks overflow. If not taken (normal path), that's 1 FP32 op per exp. If taken (overflow), there are additional FSETP and FSEL. For normal values of S (around 3.6 with small sigma), the exp argument should be small, so the normal path is taken. Per exp: 1 FSETP.GEU. Per path for 100 exps: 100 FSETP. For the payoff: DSETP.MAX (FP64, not FP32), FSEL (1 FP32). Total FP32 per path = 101. Total = 204800 × 101 = 20,684,800. However, the sqrt(dt) computation happens once. Looking at the SASS, there's a MUFU.RSQ64H which is FP64. The dsqrt helper has DFMA, DMUL etc. No significant FP32 there. So total FP32 ≈ 204800 × 101 = 20,684,800.
prediction.fp64_flop_explanation: Each path computes: (1) Constants: `r_min_half_sigma_sq_dt = (r - 0.5*sigma*sigma)*dt` = 3 FP64 ops (mul, mul, sub, mul → actually: 0.5*sigma = DMUL, *sigma = DMUL, r - ... = DSUB/DADD, *dt = DMUL = 4 ops). `sigma_sqrt_dt = sigma*sqrt(dt)` = 1 DMUL + sqrt(dt). sqrt(dt) is computed once per path. Looking at SASS for sqrt: MUFU.RSQ64H (1 FP64), then DMUL, DFMA, DFMA, DMUL, DFMA, DMUL, DFMA, DFMA = about 9 FP64 ops in the fast path. So sqrt total ≈ 9 FP64 ops. Constants total: 4 + 1 + 9 = 14 FP64 ops per path. (2) Per timestep (100 total = 99 inner loop + 1 final): each does `S = S * exp(r_min_half_sigma_sq_dt + sigma_sqrt_dt*samples[offset])`. The argument: DFMA (sigma_sqrt_dt*sample + r_min_half_sigma_sq_dt) = 2 FP64 ops (1 mul + 1 add, but DFMA = 2 FLOPs). Then exp() expansion in SASS: DFMA (arg*log2e + magic) = 2, DADD = 1, DFMA = 2, DFMA = 2, then 11 DFMA in polynomial = 22, then IMAD for scaling (integer, not FP64). Total exp ≈ 2+1+2+2+22 = 29 FP64 ops per call on normal path. Then DMUL (S * exp_result) = 1 FP64. Per timestep: 2 + 29 + 1 = 32 FP64 ops. But let me recount the SASS exp more carefully. Looking at the inner loop exp (labels .L_x_2476 area): DFMA R14, R10, R14, R8 (1 DFMA=2), DFMA R22, R14, R22, const (2), DADD R24, R22, -const (1), DFMA R26 (2), DFMA R26 (2), then 9 more DFMA (each 2) = 18, DFMA +1 = 2, DFMA +1 = 2. That's DFMA count: 13 DFMAs = 26 FP64 ops + 1 DADD = 1. Plus the initial DFMA for the argument = 2. Total in exp polynomial: 27 FP64 ops. Then DMUL R36, R26, R36 = 1 (the S*=exp result). Per timestep: DFMA(arg)=2 + exp_body=27 + DMUL(S*)=1 = 30. But wait, the DFMA R14, R10, R14, R8 IS the argument computation (sigma_sqrt_dt * sample + r_min_half_sigma_sq_dt). So per timestep: 2 (DFMA arg) + 1 (DFMA to get integer part) + ... Let me just count all DFMA/DADD/DMUL/DSUB in one loop iteration. From SASS .L_x_2476 to the STG: DFMA R14 (2), DFMA R22 (2), DADD R24 (1), DFMA R26 (2), DFMA R26 (2), DFMA R24 (2), DFMA R24 (2), DFMA R24 (2), DFMA R24 (2), DFMA R24 (2), DFMA R24 (2), DFMA R24 (2), DFMA R24 (2), DFMA R24 (2), DFMA R24 (2), DFMA R24 (2), DMUL R36 (1). That's 14 DFMAs × 2 = 28, 1 DADD = 1, 1 DMUL = 1. Total = 30 FP64 per inner iteration. For 99 inner iterations: 99 × 30 = 2970. Final iteration (after loop): same exp pattern + payoff. Exp: same 30 FP64. Payoff: DMUL R22 (S*exp) = already counted, then DADD R22 (-R22, R12) for K-S = 1 FP64. DSETP.MAX = 1 FP64 comparison. So final: 30 + 1 + 1 = 32. Per path total: 14 (constants+sqrt) + 99×30 + 32 = 14 + 2970 + 32 = 3016. Total FP64 = 204800 × 3016 = 617,676,800. But sqrt is only called for the medium path sometimes. Actually looking more carefully, the constants are computed once per path but the sqrt call may add more. The main sqrt path: MUFU.RSQ64H(1) + DMUL(1) + DFMA(2) + DFMA(2) + DMUL(1) + DFMA(2) + DMUL(1) + DFMA(2) + DFMA(2) = 14 FP64 ops. Then sigma*sqrt = DMUL(1), and the constant computation: DMUL R6 R10 -0.5 (1), DFMA R6 R6 R10 UR4 (2), DMUL R8 R6 UR4 (1). So pre-loop: 14+1+1+2+1 = 19 FP64. Total per path: 19 + 99×30 + 32 = 3021. Total = 204800 × 3021 = 618,700,800.
prediction.fp16_flop_explanation: There are HFMA2.MMA instructions at addresses 0x00a0 and 0x2990 used for constant materialization (creating small FP16 values). These are executed only by thread 0 of each block. At 0x00a0, it's in the initialization path (thread 0 only, 800 blocks). At 0x2990, it's in a code path for blocks where the number of active paths is exactly 0 (the path where R0 count equals 0, which goes to .L_x_2483). For the first invocation with 204800 paths and 800 blocks, each block has 256 paths, so most blocks will have active paths. The HFMA2 at 0x00a0 executes once per block by thread 0 = 800 times. Each HFMA2 = 4 FP16 FLOPs. At 0x2d30 there's another HFMA2.MMA in the .L_x_2494 path which is a rare divergence handler. Conservatively, the main HFMA2 at 0x00a0: 800 × 4 = 3200 FP16 FLOPs. The one at 0x2990 is in the path for blocks that go through .L_x_2483 (the 0-active-paths case), which for this workload likely doesn't execute for most blocks. Estimating ~3200 FP16 FLOPs.
prediction.dram_bytes_read_explanation: Each path reads `num_timesteps` = 100 samples (doubles, 8 bytes each) from the `samples` array: 204800 × 100 × 8 = 163,840,000 bytes. Additionally, there's one read of the PayoffPut.m_K value (from constant memory, not DRAM). The samples array is 204800 × 100 × 8 = 163,840,000 bytes total unique footprint. This is ~156 MB which far exceeds the 50 MB L2 cache, so most reads will go to DRAM. The access pattern is strided: for each timestep, all 204800 paths read consecutive elements, so it's essentially a streaming read of the full 156 MB array. DRAM bytes read ≈ 163,840,000 bytes.
prediction.dram_bytes_written_explanation: Each path writes to `paths[offset]` for each of the 100 timesteps (99 inner loop iterations + 1 final). Total writes: 204800 × 100 × 8 = 163,840,000 bytes. The unique write footprint is the same 163,840,000 bytes (~156 MB), which exceeds the 50 MB L2 cache. Since the writes are streaming (each location written once), the data will spill through L2 to DRAM. DRAM bytes written ≈ 163,840,000 bytes.

prediction.fp64_flop_explanation:
The first invocation is at timestep = num_timesteps-2 = 98. For each path (204800 total threads), the kernel does the following FP64 work:

1. Load 12 doubles from svd[] (no FLOPs).
2. Compute inv_R00, inv_R11, inv_R22: 3 conditional divisions = 3 FP64 divs (each counts as 1 FLOP for the division).
3. inv_R01 = inv_R00*inv_R11*R01: 2 muls = 2 FLOPs.
4. inv_R02 = inv_R00*inv_R22*R02: 2 muls = 2 FLOPs.
5. inv_R12 = inv_R22*R12: 1 mul = 1 FLOP.
6. inv_W00 = W00*inv_R00: 1 mul = 1 FLOP.
7. Load S = paths[path]: 0 FLOPs.
8. is_in_the_money: S < m_K → 1 comparison (not a FLOP per se, but FSETP counts; let's count it as 0 arithmetic FLOPs).
9. Q1i = inv_R11*S - inv_R01: 1 mul + 1 sub = 2 FLOPs.
10. Q2i = inv_R22*S*S - inv_R02 - Q1i*inv_R12: 3 muls + 2 subs = 5 FLOPs.
11. WI0 = inv_W00 + W01*Q1i + W02*Q2i: 2 muls + 2 adds = 4 FLOPs.
12. WI1 = W11*Q1i + W12*Q2i: 2 muls + 1 add = 3 FLOPs.
13. WI2 = W22*Q2i: 1 mul = 1 FLOP.
14. cashflow = in_the_money ? cashflows[path] : 0.0 → 0 FLOPs (conditional move).
15. beta[0] += WI0*cashflow: 1 mul + 1 add = 2 FLOPs.
16. beta[1] += WI1*cashflow: 1 mul + 1 add = 2 FLOPs.
17. beta[2] += WI2*cashflow: 1 mul + 1 add = 2 FLOPs.

Per thread: 3 (divs) + 2+2+1+1+2+5+4+3+1+2+2+2 = 30 FP64 FLOPs.

Additionally, the reduction across teams requires summing partial results for beta[0..2]. The reduction adds some overhead but is small compared to the main work.

Total: 204800 threads × 30 FLOPs = 6,144,000 FP64 FLOPs.

Note: The conditional divisions (R00 != 0.0 ? 1.0/R00 : 0.0) involve a comparison and a branch. The division itself is a complex operation that expands to many instructions in hardware. 2. Compute inv_R00, inv_R11, inv_R22: 3 conditional divisions = 3 FP64 divs (each counts as 1 FLOP for the division).
3. inv_R01 = inv_R00*inv_R11*R01: 2 muls = 2 FLOPs.
4. inv_R02 = inv_R00*inv_R22*R02: 2 muls = 2 FLOPs.
5. inv_R12 = inv_R22*R12: 1 mul = 1 FLOP.
6. inv_W00 = W00*inv_R00: 1 mul = 1 FLOP.
7. Load S = paths[path]: 0 FLOPs.
8. is_in_the_money: S < m_K → 1 comparison (not a FLOP per se, but FSETP counts; let's count it as 0 arithmetic FLOPs).
9. Q1i = inv_R11*S - inv_R01: 1 mul + 1 sub = 2 FLOPs.
10. Q2i = inv_R22*S*S - inv_R02 - Q1i*inv_R12: 3 muls + 2 subs = 5 FLOPs.
11. WI0 = inv_W00 + W01*Q1i + W02*Q2i: 2 muls + 2 adds = 4 FLOPs.
12. WI1 = W11*Q1i + W12*Q2i: 2 muls + 1 add = 3 FLOPs.
13. WI2 = W22*Q2i: 1 mul = 1 FLOP.
14. cashflow = in_the_money ? cashflows[path] : 0.0 → 0 FLOPs (conditional move).

17. beta[2] += WI2*cashflow: 1 mul + 1 add = 2 FLOPs.

prediction.gridSz_explanation: The first invocation of the target kernel occurs in do_run() at prepare_svd_kernel<256>(num_timesteps-1, num_paths, 4, ...). From main(), command line '-paths 200' overrides num_paths to 200, then the code multiplies by 1024, so num_paths=204800; num_timesteps stays at its default 100, hence numTeams=num_timesteps-1=99. The OpenMP target region uses 'teams num_teams(numTeams) thread_limit(256)', so the defensible launch estimate is 99 teams with 256 threads each, mapped to a 1-D CUDA grid/block.
prediction.blockSz_explanation: The kernel template instantiation is prepare_svd_kernel<256,...>, and the target directive explicitly sets 'thread_limit(NUM_THREADS_PER_BLOCK)'. Thus the block/team size is constrained to 256 threads in 1-D.
prediction.fp32_flop_explanation: All floating-point variables and arithmetic in this kernel and its callees are double precision; there are no float or half variables and no FP32 arithmetic visible in source. Without SASS there could be minor helper instructions in lower precision, but the best source-based estimate for executed FP32 work is zero.
prediction.fp64_flop_explanation: For the first invocation, there are 99 teams, each handling one timestep, and 256 threads per team. With default parameters for a put option (K=4, S0=3.6), all generated asset prices remain positive and every path is in-the-money at every timestep because PayoffPut::is_in_the_money(S) is S<K and the simulated path maximum over 100 steps is far below 4 for these parameters; hence all 204800 paths contribute on every timestep and the no-payoff continue path is never taken. Per team, each of the 204800 path iterations performs 7 FP64 FLOPs in the loop body when in_the_money is true: x_sq=S*S (1), sums.x+=x (1), sums.y+=x_sq (1), sums.z+=x_sq*x then += (2), sums.w+=x_sq*x_sq then += (2), totaling 7. After the loop, the team reduction contributes only 3 FP64 additions (lsums.x/y/z atomics from 256 threads; each thread adds its partial sum once), and thread 0 executes svd_3x3. Source-level counting of svd_3x3 gives 127 FP64 FLOPs outside the Jacobi loop plus assemble_R cost 101 FLOPs on the taken path where both sigma checks go to the else branch, plus 6 for off_diag_norm per loop test, plus 141 FP64 FLOPs per Jacobi iteration when all three A01/A02/A12 branches are taken, plus 22 FP64 FLOPs after the loop for swaps/inverses/U formation, plus 29 FP64 FLOPs for the no-WITH_FULL_W_MATRIX final B/W product, for a fixed-cost expression 279 + 6*(iterations+1) + 141*iterations. The matrix starts symmetric positive with nonzero off-diagonals, so a small positive iteration count is expected; using the full max_iters=16 as a defensible source-only estimate gives 2649 FP64 FLOPs for svd_3x3 per team. Total FP64 FLOPs = 99 * (204800*7 + 3 + 2649) = 141940116.
prediction.fp16_flop_explanation: The kernel uses no half-precision data or operations in source, and the called routines are all double-precision numerical code. Without SASS we do not infer any packed FP16 helper instructions here, so the best estimate is zero FP16 FLOPs.
prediction.dram_bytes_read_explanation: The only global-memory reads in the kernel are from paths[offset+path], one double per path iteration. For each of the 99 teams, the team scans all 204800 paths of its timestep exactly once, so total source-level load traffic is 99*204800*8 = 162201600 bytes. The accessed path slice over all teams spans the first 99 timesteps of d_paths, i.e. 99*204800 doubles = 161, missing? Actually 20,275,200 doubles = 162,201,600 bytes, which exceeds the 40 MB L2, and each element is read just once by its owning team, so there is essentially no inter-iteration reuse to reduce DRAM traffic; therefore DRAM read bytes are well approximated by the full streaming footprint.
prediction.dram_bytes_written_explanation: Global stores occur only at the end for teams that have enough in-the-money paths, which is true here because all 204800 paths are in the money and min_in_the_money=4. Each team writes R_W_MATRICES_SMEM_SLOTS=12 doubles to svds[16*bid + lid] for lid<12, so unique store footprint is 99*12*8 = 9504 bytes. This footprint is tiny relative to the 40 MB L2, so during this first invocation the dirty lines can remain resident in write-back L2 without eviction; under the requested DRAM model the bytes written to DRAM during the kernel are therefore estimated as zero.

prediction.gridSz_explanation: From the host code: num_paths = 200 * 1024 = 204800. NUM_THREADS_PER_BLOCK2 = 128. grid_dim = ceil(204800/128) = 1600. num_threads_per_wave_full_occupancy = 256*112 = 28672. num_waves = 1600*128/28672 ≈ 7.14. Since num_waves < 10 and fractional part 0.14 < 0.6, update_cashflow_grid = max(1, 7) * 28672 / 128 = 7*224 = 1568. The first invocation of update_cashflow_kernel uses numTeams=1568 as the grid size.
prediction.blockSz_explanation: The kernel template parameter NUM_THREADS_PER_BLOCK is 128, and the pragma specifies thread_limit(NUM_THREADS_PER_BLOCK), so blockSz = 128.
prediction.fp32_flop_explanation: Looking at the SASS, there are FSEL instructions (FP32 select) which are not arithmetic FLOPs. No FP32 arithmetic (FADD, FMUL, FFMA) instructions appear on the main execution path. The FSEL is a conditional select, not an arithmetic operation. So FP32 FLOPs = 0.
prediction.fp64_flop_explanation:
Analyzing the kernel: num_paths = 204800, total threads = 1568*128 = 200704. The kernel uses a grid-stride loop. Looking at the SASS, the kernel has a complex structure with multiple code paths. Each thread processes paths in a grid-stride pattern. Total paths = 204800, total threads = 200704, so most threads process 1 path, and 204800-200704=4096 threads process a 2nd path iteration (but looking at the SASS more carefully, the loop structure uses a different stride pattern based on the OpenMP distribute parallel for).

Actually, with `teams distribute parallel for` and num_teams(1568) thread_limit(128), the iteration space of 204800 is distributed. Each team gets ceil(204800/1568)=131 or 130 iterations, distributed among 128 threads per team. So each thread handles ~1 iteration (some handle 2).

Per path iteration (non-skip path): The kernel reads all_out_of_the_money (skip_computations). If skip_computations=0: loads S from paths, computes S2=S*S (1 DMUL), payoff = fmax(K-S, 0.0) which is DADD (K-S = 1 DADD with negation, so the DADD R8, -R10, R8 counts as 1 FP64 op), then fmax (DSETP.MAX). estimated_payoff = beta0 + beta1*S + beta2*S2 = 2 DFMA + 1 DADD or looking at SASS: DFMA R12, R10, R12, R14 (beta1*S + beta0), DFMA R12, R20, R24, R12 (beta2*S2 + prev), then DMUL R12, R12, exp_min_r_dt. Also DMUL for old_cashflow = exp_min_r_dt * cashflows[path].

From SASS per iteration on the non-skip path: DMUL (old_cashflow), DADD (K-S), DSETP.MAX, DMUL (S*S), DFMA, DFMA, DMUL (estimated_payoff *= exp_min_r_dt), DSETP.GTU. That's 3 DMUL + 1 DADD + 2 DFMA + 2 DSETP = 3+1+4+0 = 8 FP64 FLOPs (DFMA = 2 each, DMUL=1, DADD=1, DSETP comparisons are not FLOPs typically). Actually DSETP comparisons don't count as FLOPs. So: 3 DMUL (3 FLOPs) + 1 DADD (1 FLOP) + 2 DFMA (4 FLOPs) = 8 FP64 FLOPs per path.

But we need to know how many paths take the non-skip vs skip path. The first invocation is for timestep = num_timesteps-2 = 98. Whether all_out_of_the_money[98] is 0 or 1 depends on data. Assuming it's 0 (not all out of money), all 204800 paths execute the full computation.

Total FP64 FLOPs = 204800 * 8 = 1,638,400. But some paths may have payoff <= 1e-8 and skip the beta load/compute. Looking more carefully, the beta computation only happens when payoff > 1e-8 (DSETP.GTU check). For paths not in the money, payoff=0 so they skip. But we still have DMUL for old_cashflow and DADD+DSETP for payoff computation.

For all 204800 paths: DMUL (1) + DADD (1) = 2 FP64 FLOPs minimum. For in-the-money paths additionally: DMUL(S*S) + DFMA + DFMA + DMUL(estimated*exp) = 1+2+2+1 = 6 more. Since this is data-dependent, I'll estimate conservatively that roughly half are in the money: ~102400 * 6 + 204800 * 2 = 614400 + 409600 = 1,024,000. But this is uncertain. Given the put option with K=4, S0=3.6, many paths will be in the money. Let me estimate ~75% in the money: 153600*8 + 51200*2 = 1,228,800 + 102,400 = 1,331,200. This is very data-dependent. I'll estimate all paths go through the full path for a reasonable upper estimate: 204800 * 8 = 1,638,400.
prediction.fp16_flop_explanation: The SASS shows HFMA2.MMA instructions used for zero/constant materialization. At address 0x0280, HFMA2.MMA R23, -RZ, RZ, 0, 0 executes once per outer loop iteration per thread. At 0x0fb0, HFMA2.MMA R0, -RZ, RZ, 0, 5.96e-08 appears in one code path. Also in __cuda_sm70_barrier_sync_8 at 0x0020, HFMA2.MMA R4, -RZ, RZ, 0, 0. Each HFMA2 = 4 FP16 FLOPs. The HFMA2 at 0x0280 executes in the main loop. With grid-stride looping, each thread executes the outer loop once (since 200704 threads ≈ 204800 paths, roughly 1 iteration). So ~200704 * 4 = 802816 FP16 FLOPs from that instruction. The other HFMA2 instructions execute conditionally. Estimating conservatively: ~200704 threads execute the 0x0280 HFMA2 once = 802816 FP16 FLOPs.
prediction.dram_bytes_read_explanation: The kernel reads: (1) all_out_of_the_money[timestep]: 4 bytes, loaded by LDG.E, one int per path but same address so cached after first load = 1 cache line = 32 bytes. (2) cashflows[path]: 204800 * 8 = 1,638,400 bytes. (3) paths[path]: 204800 * 8 = 1,638,400 bytes for paths at the given timestep offset. (4) beta[0..2]: 3 doubles = 24 bytes, same for all threads, fits in one cache line = 32 bytes. Total unique read footprint ≈ 1,638,400 + 1,638,400 + 64 = 3,276,864 bytes. This is ~3.1 MB which fits well within the 40 MB L2 cache, so DRAM reads equal the unique footprint (compulsory misses). Rounding to cache-line granularity: cashflows = 204800*8/128 * 128 = 1,638,400 bytes, paths similarly. Total DRAM reads ≈ 3,276,864 bytes.
prediction.dram_bytes_written_explanation: The kernel writes cashflows[path] for each of the 204800 paths: 204800 * 8 = 1,638,400 bytes. The unique write footprint is ~1.56 MB which fits entirely in the 40 MB L2 cache. Since the L2 is write-back and the footprint fits in cache, no evictions to DRAM are expected during this kernel invocation. DRAM bytes written ≈ 0.

prediction.gridSz_explanation: The kernel is `compute_beta_kernel<128, PayoffPut>`. From the host code, `num_paths = 200 * 1024 = 204800`. The kernel uses `#pragma omp target teams distribute parallel for thread_limit(128) reduction(+:beta[:3])`. The loop iterates over `num_paths = 204800` paths. However, this kernel is called inside a loop `for timestep = num_timesteps-2 down to 0`, and the first invocation is at `timestep = num_timesteps-2 = 98`. The kernel has an early exit check `if(*all_out_of_the_money == 0)` before the parallel region. The grid size for OpenMP target teams distribute parallel for is runtime-determined. With 204800 iterations and 128 threads per block, a natural grid would be ceil(204800/128) = 1600 teams. However, the OpenMP runtime on this architecture typically launches this as a single CGA or uses a grid-stride pattern. Looking at the SASS more carefully, the kernel structure is very complex with atomic reductions, shared memory coordination, and a multi-phase approach (inner loop over paths with grid-stride, then warp/block reductions, then cross-block atomic accumulation). The SASS shows `R48 = c[0x0][0xc]` which is the num_teams parameter from the runtime. The grid-stride loop pattern `R60 = R63 * 0x80 + R60` (where 0x80 = 128) and comparison against UR38 (num_paths-1) suggests the runtime launches fewer teams than ceil(num_paths/128). Given the OpenMP runtime behavior on H100 for reductions, a common choice is to use a moderate number of teams. Based on the SASS evidence showing grid-stride execution and the reduction pattern, the runtime likely launches around 1600 teams (ceil(204800/128)), but could also be fewer. I'll estimate 1600 as the most natural mapping.

But many paths won't be in the money (S0=3.6, K=4.0, put option, so S<K means in the money). With random paths, many will be in the money. For a rough estimate, assume ~50% are in the money on average across timesteps. Per iteration: ~5 FP64 ops × probability. But the scan also has no FP64 ops. The sums.w accumulation seems missing from SASS (only x,y,z accumulated). So per in-the-money path: 5 FP64 ops. Total threads = 99 × 256 = 25344. Each thread does 800 iterations. With ~50% in the money: 25344 × 800 × 0.5 × 5 = 50,688,000 FP64 ops from the loop. Then thread 0 in each of 99 blocks executes svd_3x3 which has hundreds of FP64 ops (assemble_R + eigenvalue iterations + final computation). Estimating ~500-1000 FP64 ops per block for svd_3x3. 99 × 800 = 79200 FP64 ops from svd. Total ≈ 50,688,000 + 79,200 ≈ 50,767,200. However, this is very data-dependent. I'll estimate ~50,700,000.
args.fp16_flop_explanation: Looking at SASS, there are HFMA2.MMA instructions used for constant materialization (e.g., at 0x3790, 0x3930, 0x41a0, 0x9c90, 0x9e30, 0xa6a0). Also the barrier_sync HFMA2 is called many times. For 99 blocks, thread 0 executes ~6 HFMA2 in the Jacobi section (3 per Jacobi rotation setup × some iterations). args.dram_bytes_read_explanation: Each block reads paths for its timestep. prediction.gridSz_explanation: The kernel is `compute_beta_kernel<128, PayoffPut>`. From the host code in `do_run`, the loop runs from `timestep = num_timesteps-2` down to 0. The first invocation is at `timestep = num_timesteps-2 = 98`. The kernel uses `#pragma omp target teams distribute parallel for thread_limit(128) reduction(+:beta[:3])`. With num_paths = 200*1024 = 204800, the OpenMP runtime distributes the iteration space. Looking at the SASS, the kernel uses a complex grid-stride loop pattern with CTAID.X-based work distribution. The SASS shows `R52 = R19 << 7` (CTAID.X * 128) and checks against num_paths (204800). The grid size for `teams distribute parallel for` with 204800 iterations and 128 threads per block would be ceil(204800/128) = 1600 teams. However, OpenMP runtimes on NVIDIA GPUs typically launch exactly ceil(N/blockSize) teams for `teams distribute parallel for`. So gridSz = [1600, 1, 1].
prediction.blockSz_explanation: The template parameter NUM_THREADS_PER_BLOCK2 = 128 is used as the thread_limit in the OpenMP pragma, so blockSz = [128, 1, 1].
prediction.fp32_flop_explanation: Looking at the SASS, there are no FP32 arithmetic instructions (FADD, FMUL, FFMA) on the main execution path. There are no FP32 FLOPs in this kernel.

But each thread processes exactly 1 path (204800 paths / 204800 threads). So the loop body executes once per thread.

prediction.gridSz_explanation: The kernel is `compute_beta_kernel<128, PayoffPut>`. The OpenMP runtime for clang offload typically creates teams based on the iteration space. Looking at the SASS, the kernel uses a complex structure with grid-stride loops and team-based reduction. Given the `teams distribute parallel for` with 128 threads and 204800 iterations, the runtime would typically launch ceil(204800/128) = 1600 teams. However, the SASS shows a grid-stride pattern where each CTA processes multiple chunks of 128 paths. The runtime may choose fewer teams. Given the OpenMP runtime behavior for clang on NVIDIA GPUs, a common choice is ceil(num_paths/128) = 1600 teams.

1. `all_out_of_the_money[timestep]`: 1 int = 4 bytes. This is checked on the host before the kernel launch (the `if(*all_out_of_the_money == 0)` check is on the host side). Actually, looking more carefully, this check happens on the host before the OpenMP target region. So the kernel only launches if the condition is met.

2. `svd[]`: 12 doubles (indices 0-11, no WITH_FULL_W_MATRIX) = 96 bytes. These are read by every thread but are the same values, so they'll be cached. Unique footprint = 96 bytes (one cache line of 128 bytes).

3. `paths[path]`: Each thread reads one double. 204800 * 8 = 1,638,400 bytes unique footprint.

4. `cashflows[path]`: Each thread conditionally reads one double. Up to 204800 * 8 = 1,638,400 bytes unique footprint.

Total unique read footprint: ~96 + 1,638,400 + 1,638,400 ≈ 3,276,896 bytes ≈ 3.1 MB.

The L2 cache is 6 MB, so the entire read footprint fits in L2. However, this is the first access to these arrays by this kernel, so compulsory misses will cause DRAM reads for the full unique footprint. The paths and cashflows data were written by previous kernels (generate_paths_kernel and prepare_svd_kernel), so they may already be in L2. The svd data (96 bytes) was written by prepare_svd_kernel. The cashflows are actually `h_paths + (num_timesteps-1)*num_paths`, which is the last portion of the paths array written by generate_paths_kernel.

Since the total working set of previous kernels is much larger (paths array = 100*204800*8 = ~156 MB), the L2 (6 MB) would have been thrashed. So the data for this timestep likely needs to be fetched from DRAM.

DRAM bytes read ≈ 128 (svd, rounded to cache line) + 1,638,400 (paths for timestep 98) + 1,638,400 (cashflows) ≈ 3,276,928 bytes.
args.dram_bytes_written_explanation:
The kernel writes to `beta[0:3]` which is 3 doubles = 24 bytes. This is done via a reduction, so the final result is 24 bytes. With the reduction pattern in OpenMP, each team may write partial sums to temporary storage, but the final output is just 3 doubles.

With 1600 teams doing a reduction, the runtime likely allocates temporary storage for partial results: 1600 * 3 * 8 = 38,400 bytes for team-level partial sums, plus the final 24 bytes. The total write footprint is approximately 38,424 bytes.

This easily fits in the 6 MB L2 cache, so DRAM bytes written during this kernel invocation would be approximately 0, as the dirty cache lines remain in L2 until eviction by later kernels. However, the `d_temp_storage` array (the beta output) is 4*2048*8 = 65,536 bytes total allocation, which fits in L2.

DRAM bytes written ≈ 0 since the write footprint is tiny and fits in L2.

metrics_explanations.gridSz_explanation: The kernel `compute_beta_kernel<128, PayoffPut>` is launched with `#pragma omp target teams distribute parallel for thread_limit(128) reduction(+:beta[:3])`. The loop iterates over `num_paths = 200 * 1024 = 204800` paths. The OpenMP runtime distributes this loop across teams. With `ceil(204800 / 128) = 1600` iterations per block, the grid size would be 1600 teams. However, OpenMP runtimes on NVIDIA GPUs typically create one team per loop chunk. With 204800 iterations and 128 threads per team, we get ceil(204800/128) = 1600 teams. This is the first invocation at timestep = num_timesteps-2 = 98.
metrics_explanations.blockSz_explanation: The `thread_limit(128)` clause in the pragma sets the block size to 128 threads. NUM_THREADS_PER_BLOCK2 = 128.
metrics_explanations.fp32_flop_explanation: There are no single-precision floating point operations in this kernel. All arithmetic is done in double precision (FP64). Some compiler-generated FP32 instructions might exist for control flow or address computation, but these would be minimal.
metrics_explanations.fp64_flop_explanation:
Each thread (204800 total) executes the compute_beta_kernel body. Let me count FP64 operations per thread:

Loading svd values: no FLOPs.
inv_R00: 1 division (conditional, but likely taken for most cases) = 1 FLOP
inv_R11: 1 division = 1 FLOP  
inv_R22: 1 division = 1 FLOP
inv_R01: inv_R00*inv_R11 (1 mul) * R01 (1 mul) = 2 FLOPs
inv_R02: inv_R00*inv_R22 (1 mul) * R02 (1 mul) = 2 FLOPs
inv_R12: inv_R22*R12 = 1 FLOP
inv_W00: W00*inv_R00 = 1 FLOP (no WITH_FULL_W_MATRIX)

S = paths[path]: load, no FLOP
in_the_money = payoff.is_in_the_money(S) => S < m_K: 1 comparison (not FP FLOP per se, but FP compare). Let's count it as 0 FLOPs (comparisons are typically DSETP, not arithmetic).

Q1i = inv_R11*S - inv_R01: 1 mul + 1 sub = 2 FLOPs
Q2i = inv_R22*S*S - inv_R02 - Q1i*inv_R12: inv_R22*S (1 mul), *S (1 mul), - inv_R02 (1 sub), Q1i*inv_R12 (1 mul), subtract (1 sub) = 5 FLOPs

WI0 = inv_W00 + W01*Q1i + W02*Q2i: 2 muls + 2 adds = 4 FLOPs
WI1 = W11*Q1i + W12*Q2i: 2 muls + 1 add = 3 FLOPs
WI2 = W22*Q2i: 1 mul = 1 FLOP

cashflow = in_the_money ? cashflows[path] : 0.0: conditional load, 0 FLOPs

beta[0] += WI0*cashflow: 1 mul + 1 add = 2 FLOPs
beta[1] += WI1*cashflow: 1 mul + 1 add = 2 FLOPs
beta[2] += WI2*cashflow: 1 mul + 1 add = 2 FLOPs

Also the comparisons R00 != 0.0, R11 != 0.0, R22 != 0.0 for conditional divisions: these are FP comparisons, not arithmetic FLOPs.

Total per thread: 1+1+1+2+2+1+1+2+5+4+3+1+2+2+2 = 30 FP64 FLOPs per thread.

Additionally, the reduction across teams requires summing partial results. But the main arithmetic is 30 FLOPs per thread.

Total: 204800 * 30 = 6,144,000 FP64 FLOPs.

However, the conditional divisions (ternary with != 0.0 check) still execute the division in most cases. Let me count them as 1 FLOP each (3 total). Already counted above.

Total FP64 FLOPs = 204800 * 30 = 6,144,000.

records.kernel_demangled_name: void generate_paths_kernel<(int)256, PayoffPut>(int, int, T2, double, double, double, double, const double *, double *):l97

prediction.gridSz_explanation: From main(), the command line '-paths 200' sets num_paths=200, then host code multiplies by 1024 before do_run(), so the first invocation sees num_paths=204800. The target kernel is an OpenMP 'teams distribute parallel for thread_limit(256)' over path in [0,num_paths), and the SASS shows CTAID.X shifted by 8 (×256) with a grid-stride style outer loop, so the team size is 256 and the runtime only needs enough CTAs to cover the iteration space; the most defensible first-launch estimate is ceil(204800/256)=800 teams.
prediction.blockSz_explanation: The kernel template instantiation is generate_paths_kernel<256,...> and the OpenMP directive uses thread_limit(NUM_THREADS_PER_BLOCK). The SASS also hard-codes a left shift by 8 for CTA base indexing, confirming 256 threads per team/block.
prediction.fp32_flop_explanation: Neither source nor SASS show any FP16/FP32 arithmetic on the taken path; all floating-point arithmetic is double precision (DMUL/DFMA/etc.). Therefore FP32 FLOPs are zero for this kernel invocation.
prediction.fp64_flop_explanation: For each path/thread, setup computes r_min_half_sigma_sq_dt=(r-0.5*sigma*sigma)*dt (3 FLOPs: sigma*sigma, multiply by 0.5, subtract; final multiply by dt is fused later in SASS accounting here as one more op => 4 total) and sigma_sqrt_dt=sigma*sqrt(dt). The SASS for sqrt(dt) executes a MUFU.RSQ64H + 8 double ops in-kernel and, for this input dt=0.01, takes the mediumpath helper with 5 more FP64 ops, so sqrt contributes 14 FP64 ops including the final multiply by sigma; each timestep update executes sigma_sqrt_dt*samples[offset] (1), add r_min_half_sigma_sq_dt (1), exp() lowered in SASS to 2 DMUL + 13 DFMA = 28 FP64 FLOPs on the normal taken path, then multiply by S (1), for 31 FP64 FLOPs per timestep. With num_timesteps=100 there are 100 such updates per path (99 loop iterations plus final one), and the final PayoffPut computes K-S plus max with 0.0, counting one FP64 subtraction; total per path = 4 + 14 + 100*31 + 1 = 3119 FP64 FLOPs, scaled over 204800 paths gives 638771200.
prediction.fp16_flop_explanation: The kernel uses only double-precision data and the provided SASS contains no FP16 arithmetic instructions on the executed path. Therefore FP16 FLOPs are zero.
prediction.dram_bytes_read_explanation: Each path consumes one Gaussian sample per timestep from 'samples[offset]' and there are 100 timesteps, so source-level traffic is 204800*100 double loads = 20,480,000 loads = 163,840,000 bytes. The access pattern streams through the entire 156.25 MiB samples array once with essentially no temporal reuse inside the invocation, far exceeding the 6 MiB L2, so DRAM read bytes are well-approximated by this full streaming load volume.
prediction.dram_bytes_written_explanation: Each path writes one double to 'paths[offset]' per timestep, again 100 stores per path, so total store traffic is 20,480,000 double stores = 163,840,000 bytes. The written footprint is also about 156.25 MiB, much larger than the 6 MiB L2, and the kernel streams through distinct cache lines, so those dirty lines will be evicted during the invocation; thus DRAM writes are approximated by the full output footprint.
